authors: Sujatha, R., Krishnan, S., Chatterjee, J. M., and Gandomi, A. H.
title: Advancing plant leaf disease detection integrating machine learning and deep learning
access: Publisher article and relevant methods and results reviewed

short: Lightweight transfer learning on our dataset
title: Potato Leaf Disease Detection Based on a Lightweight Deep Learning Model
summary: This study adapts RegNetY-400MF to the same 3,076-image potato collection. It investigates transfer learning, learning rate, batch size and image augmentation. Its chosen settings include a batch size of 16 and learning rate of 0.001.
result: The paper reports a highest individual test accuracy of 90.68%. Its lightweight-model cross-validation comparison reports mean accuracy 89.87% with standard deviation 1.28. These are distinct summaries. It also reports 0.40 GFLOPs, 16.8 MB and 4,344,144 parameters.
use: This is our most important additional compact-model reference. It establishes that 62.6% is not the strongest reported result on this collection. RegNetY is a possible additional comparator if the team expands the experiment.
limit: Section 3.7 describes best validation accuracies across folds. This differs from our reserved final test set. Actual edge-device inference timing is left to future work; compactness alone does not establish measured deployment speed.

short: A CNN and Transformer on field images
authors: Mondal, A., Chatterjee, A., and Avazov, N.
title: A hybrid CNN-transformer model with adaptive activation function for potato leaf disease classification
access: Publisher methods results and limitations reviewed
summary: PLDNet combines an ImageNet-pretrained DenseNet169 backbone, a Transformer component and an adaptive AFpM activation function. The authors train separately on PlantVillage and Mendeley using 80:20 stratified train/test splits.
result: The statistical section reports five random-split experiments, with average accuracy 99.54% on PlantVillage and 87.50% on Mendeley. The architecture contains approximately 32 million trainable parameters. Publication was 6 January 2026, despite the DOI containing 025.
use: Use this study to motivate a measured trade-off between architecture complexity, prediction quality and computational cost. Its larger architecture provides context for our proposed smaller CNN.
limit: The authors explicitly did not train on one dataset and test on the other. Independent training on two datasets does not establish cross-domain transfer. Clarify its validation allocation before reproducing validation-based callbacks.

short: The origin of our potato dataset
authors: Shabrina, N. H., Indarti, S., Maharani, R., Kristiyanti, D. A., Irmawati, Prastomo, N., and M, T. A.
year: 2024 issue with first online publication in 2023
title: A novel dataset of potato leaf disease in uncontrolled environment
access: Publisher metadata and open full text in PMC reviewed
summary: The dataset article explains the collection of 3,076 smartphone images from potato farms in Central Java, Indonesia. It describes seven categories and variable backgrounds, viewpoints and capture conditions. The images are 1,500 by 1,500 pixels.
result: Its initial benchmarks compare pretrained CNNs. EfficientNetV2B3 reports 73.63% test accuracy without augmentation; Table 7 reports 72.35% with augmentation. The study first makes a 90:10 train/test split, then takes validation images from training.
use: Read this before discussing dataset provenance, labels or field conditions. It also demonstrates why augmentation must be tested rather than assumed beneficial. Dataset DOI: 10.17632/ptz377bwb8.1; licence: CC BY 4.0.
limit: The journal issue is February 2024, but first online publication was 12 December 2023. Its original image selection and split differ from our cleaned manifest. The dataset categories are broad; predictions do not confirm a precise pathogen.

short: Reweighting for an imbalanced potato task
authors: Jlassi, A., Elaoud, A., Ghazouani, H., and Barhoumi, W.
title: Potato Leaf Disease Classification Using Transfer Learning and Reweighting-Based Training with Imbalanced Data
access: Publisher abstract only subscription full text unavailable
summary: The abstract describes MobileNetV2 fine-tuning, image augmentation, explainability and a reweighting method on PlantVillage.
result: The abstract reports 98.61% classification accuracy. This is not a seven-category Mendeley result.
use: This is direct precedent for testing class weighting. Our weighted-loss experiment applies an established technique; it is not a new invention.
limit: The exact reweighting formula, class selection and evaluation partition were not verified. Obtain institutional full text before describing or reproducing those details.

authors: Talab, H. K., Mohammadzamani, D., and Parashkoohi, M. G.
title: Investigating the accuracy of classification in unbalanced data in order to diagnose two common potato leaf diseases (early blight and late blight) using image processing and machine learning
access: Publisher full text and relevant methods reviewed
summary: The authors collect 1,900 potato images: 550 healthy, 350 early blight and 1,000 late blight. They extract colour, texture and shape features, use Random Forest classification and study over- and undersampling. The stated split is 80% training and 20% testing.
result: Reported accuracies are 87.89% for original data, 91.09% for oversampling and 96.17% for undersampling. The work also studies Relief feature selection.
use: This supports evaluating imbalance strategies using category-level measurements. Weighting the loss and changing sampling frequencies are different interventions and should be compared separately.
limit: It uses another collection and only three categories. Check whether evaluation composition changes under resampling before attributing every accuracy difference to learning improvements. Undersampling discards examples.

short: Preprocessing and imbalance in a pipeline
authors: Ojo, M. O., and Zahid, A.
title: Improving Deep Learning Classifiers Performance via Preprocessing and Class Imbalance Approaches in a Plant Disease Detection Pipeline
access: Publisher text and relevant pipeline sections reviewed
summary: This study examines bacterial-wilt recognition in greenhouse tomato images. It compares histogram enhancement, sharpening and resampling methods including SMOTE, major-to-minor translation and GAN-based generation, with several CNN classifiers.
result: The authors report average classification accuracy 97.69% and average F1-score 97.62% for their strongest ResNet50 pipeline combining CLAHE, sharpening and GAN-based resampling.
use: It motivates controlled experiments on input preprocessing and class balance, in addition to architecture. Add one intervention at a time so its effect can be measured.
limit: This is a different crop and task under greenhouse conditions. Its performance does not establish gains on seven-category field images. Synthetic augmentation adds complexity and must remain within training partitions; it is outside our initial core scope.

authors: Ahmad, M., Abdullah, M., Moon, H., and Han, D.
title: Plant Disease Detection in Imbalanced Datasets Using Efficient Convolutional Neural Networks With Stepwise Transfer Learning
access: Publisher indexed abstract and method excerpts reviewed
summary: The paper studies efficient CNN classification, class balancing and stepwise transfer learning on PlantVillage and a pepper-disease dataset. Its training approach progressively releases pretrained layers for adaptation rather than updating every layer immediately.
result: The abstract reports accuracy of 99% on the pepper dataset and 99.69% on PlantVillage. These are the authors’ results on their tasks, not targets established for our dataset.
use: This is relevant to limited data, training efficiency and portable models. If scratch training is weak, gradual fine-tuning can be investigated as a clearly documented additional experiment.
limit: The exact balancing rule and training schedule require verification from the complete paper before replication. Transfer learning is a different experimental condition from our proposed CNN trained from scratch.

short: Learning useful regions in complex images
authors: Liu, X., Min, W., Mei, S., Wang, L., and Jiang, S.
title: Plant Disease Recognition: A Large-Scale Benchmark Dataset and a Visual Region and Loss Reweighting Approach
access: Publisher indexed abstract and author institution summary reviewed
summary: The authors introduce a 220,592-image benchmark containing 271 disease categories. Their approach weights image regions and patch-label training losses, then aggregates patch features using an LSTM to represent the image.
result: The reviewed abstract describes evaluations on their collection and another public dataset. No numerical score is reproduced here because the full result tables were not verified.
use: This provides a concrete explanation of why randomly positioned lesions and cluttered backgrounds can be difficult. It motivates inspecting whether our CNN uses relevant leaf features.
limit: Patch-level and region-level loss weighting are not the same as our category-frequency weights. The larger framework and dataset are supporting research; reproducing the complete system is outside our initial project scope.

authors: Arshad, F., Mateen, M., Hayat, S., Wardah, M., Al-Huda, Z., Gu, Y. H., and Al-antari, M. A.
title: PLDPNet: End-to-end hybrid deep learning framework for potato leaf disease prediction
access: Publisher indexed abstract and author institution record reviewed
summary: PLDPNet combines preprocessing, segmentation, deep feature extraction and feature fusion. Features from VGG19 and InceptionV3 are combined, with a Transformer-based stage used for prediction. The potato experiment covers early blight, late blight and healthy leaves.
result: The abstract reports 98.66% potato accuracy and 96.33% F1-score. It also describes separate apple and tomato experiments. Those experiments do not establish transfer to our seven potato categories.
use: Use this to discuss complementary feature representations and the design of a complete image pipeline. It is a more complex alternative to the separate feature-extractor and SVM baseline.
limit: Exact split construction and ablation tables were not verified from full text. Measure total inference cost if adopting feature fusion or segmentation; extra stages can add latency and implementation burden.

authors: Kasana, S. S., and Rathore, A. S.
title: Attention-Based Light Weight Deep Learning Models for Early Potato Disease Detection
access: Publisher indexed abstract and detailed indexed excerpts reviewed
summary: This study compares attention-based variants of DenseNet169, Xception, MobileNet and VGG16. Channel and spatial attention emphasise useful information while the classifier design is reduced. It combines PlantVillage and PLD for a three-category potato task.
result: The paper describes similar predictive performance with fewer trainable parameters. No single headline accuracy is reproduced here: the indexed tables distinguish training, validation and testing, and parameter reductions vary by architecture.
use: This motivates measuring parameter count alongside predictive quality. A smaller model may be worthwhile even if its accuracy is similar rather than higher.
limit: Direct publisher retrieval was blocked during verification; the reading is based on indexed excerpts. Reconcile the text’s augmentation descriptions and check original-image independence before reproducing the merged dataset procedure.

title: Comparative Evaluation of Deep Features and Traditional Classifiers in the Detection of Potato Leaf Diseases
access: Publisher abstract and relevant methods reviewed
summary: The study compares CNN feature extractors including VGG19, ResNet50, Xception, MobileNetV2 and DenseNet121 with traditional and neural classifiers. It describes two balanced 3,000-image collections, PlantVillage and field-collected Beunto, with three potato categories.
result: ResNet50 with DNN-3 reports 98.56% on PlantVillage and 98.20% on Beunto in within-dataset experiments. These numbers must not be relabelled as cross-dataset transfer accuracy. The methods describe an 80:20 split and additional runs.
use: This is especially relevant to Phase III: the feature representation and the classifier each influence performance. A stronger classifier cannot be assumed to repair poor features.
limit: The described balanced PlantVillage selection needs reconciliation with the familiar smaller raw healthy category before reproduction. It is not our seven-category collection. Verify the cross-dataset results separately from the abstract’s within-dataset scores.

short: A small model with channel attention
authors: Askale, G. T., Yibel, A. B., Taye, B. M., and Wubneh, G. D.
title: An attention-enhanced MobileNetV2 with squeeze-and-excitation architecture for efficient potato leaf disease detection and classification
summary: The model adds squeeze-and-excitation attention to MobileNetV2 and uses Grad-CAM to visualise influential regions. Its experiment uses 2,152 Kaggle potato images covering early blight, late blight and healthy leaves.
result: The abstract describes 70% training, 20% validation and 10% testing, and reports 99% test accuracy. This result is for a three-category task, not our seven categories.
use: This supports investigating channel attention and explainability if the core project is complete. It illustrates a compact transfer-learning route rather than training every model from zero.
limit: Only the accessible abstract was reviewed. The exact architecture, preprocessing and deployment timing require full-method verification. A heatmap and high benchmark accuracy do not establish dependable performance on unfamiliar field photographs.

short: Classification with multiple leaves and clutter
authors: Xie, K., Xu, D., and Chang, S.
title: Self-Attention-Enhanced Deep Learning Framework with Multi-Scale Feature Fusion for Potato Disease Detection in Complex Multi-Leaf Field Conditions
summary: ResNet18-SAWF adds self-attention and multi-scale feature fusion to ResNet18. The study combines public potato images with a separately collected ground dataset and examines single-leaf and complex multi-leaf images across three categories.
result: The authors report 98.36% accuracy in their complex-background multi-leaf classification experiment, compared with 91.80% for the corresponding ResNet18 baseline in that experiment.
use: This helps explain the difference between clean single-leaf images and photographs containing several leaves and background objects. It motivates error analysis by image conditions.
limit: These are image-classification results, not a bounding-box detection score or proof of generalisation to our dataset. Its data construction differs from ours, so reproduce its exact comparison before making architecture-effect claims.

short: An explainable ensemble on field photographs
authors: Verma, K., Dubey, M. K., and Pandey, D. K.
title: Application of Explainable AI-Driven Ensemble Modelling Approach for Robust Potato Disease Identification under Field Conditions
access: Publisher abstract only subscription full text unavailable
summary: The abstract describes an ensemble using several CNN architectures with explainability. Its source collection contains 2,017 field photographs from Punjab, India, augmented to 7,248 samples, covering early blight, late blight and healthy leaves.
result: The abstract reports 99.72% accuracy on an independent test set. This has not been independently reproduced here.
use: It provides a potato-specific example of combining field data, transfer learning and visual explanations. Ensemble benefits should be weighed against the cost of all participating models.
limit: The full text was not accessible. Original-image separation, augmentation order, detailed ensemble construction and measured inference time remain unverified. Do not treat the reported percentage as a benchmark for our seven-category task.

authors: Jain, A., Dubey, A. K., Singh, S. K., Panwar, A., Gupta, N., Kumar, S., Arya, V., Alhalabi, W., Pan, S.-H., Alsulami, B. S., and Gupta, B. B.
title: Optimized CNN-based ensemble deep learning approach for potato leaf disease detection with data augmentation
summary: The study combines CNNs trained with Adam, SGD, RMSprop and Adamax. It uses three PlantVillage potato categories: 1,000 early-blight images, 1,000 late-blight images and 152 healthy images, with augmentation to address imbalance.
result: The EDL10 ensemble reports 97% accuracy. The paper describes an 80:20 split with a further validation allocation from training.
use: This motivates controlled experiments on optimization and augmentation. It also shows why the deployment cost of an ensemble must include every model rather than only the final combination step.
limit: Parts of the pipeline description place balancing before splitting. Verify whether derived images from the same original are separated correctly before replication; the description alone is not proof that leakage occurred. Our procedure splits first and augments training only.

short: Why benchmark accuracy can fail on new images
authors: Mohanty, S. P., Hughes, D. P., and Salathé, M.
title: Using Deep Learning for Image-Based Plant Disease Detection
access: Publisher full text and external image evaluation reviewed
summary: This foundational study trains CNNs on 54,306 PlantVillage images spanning 38 crop-condition categories. It also evaluates models on two small collections of images obtained from external online sources.
result: The strongest PlantVillage result is 99.35% held-out accuracy. On the two external collections containing 121 and 119 images, reported accuracy is 31.40% and 31.69%, respectively, over the 38-category task.
use: This is a clear reason to separate performance on a benchmark from performance on new acquisition conditions. It supports honest limits on our upload application and the need for independent field testing.
limit: The external samples are small, and its task differs from ours. These values do not predict our accuracy. The lesson is the observed sensitivity to image distribution, not that all CNNs necessarily perform poorly outside PlantVillage.

authors: Selvaraju, R. R., Cogswell, M., Das, A., Vedantam, R., Parikh, D., and Batra, D.
year: 2020 journal issue with first online publication in 2019
title: Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-Based Localization
access: Springer journal version and author manuscript reviewed
summary: Grad-CAM uses gradients of a selected class score with respect to convolutional feature maps to produce a coarse map of influential image regions. The journal version extends the well-known conference work and applies the technique to multiple vision tasks.
result: This is an explanation-method paper, not a potato classifier. A single potato accuracy percentage would therefore be an inappropriate summary of its contribution.
use: Apply Grad-CAM to a trained CNN to inspect successful and failed predictions. It may reveal reliance on backgrounds or hands. The separate feature-extractor and SVM pipeline needs an appropriate explanation method rather than assuming the CNN procedure transfers unchanged.
limit: A plausible heatmap is not proof of a correct diagnosis or a causal explanation. The map is coarse. Report it as qualitative supporting evidence alongside numerical evaluation, not as an accuracy improvement by itself.
